explain.title: Group 1 elements have one outermost-shell electron
explain.body: All the elements present in group 1 have ns¹ configuration in their outermost shells. They are also called alkali metals. Because the single outer electron can be removed easily, these metals are very reactive. Hydrogen is the exception: it is a gas and a non-metal.

explain.title: Reactivity increases down Group 1
explain.body: Atomic size increases down the group. The outer electron is then easier to lose, so the lower members are more reactive. For example, lithium reacts steadily with water, sodium vigorously and potassium violently.

explain.title: The metals become softer and their melting points decrease
explain.body: Increasing atomic size weakens the interatomic attraction of the atoms in the metals. The metals become softer down the group, and their melting points decrease.

explain.title: Density generally increases down the group
explain.body: Both atomic size and mass increase down the group. The increase in mass is greater than the increase in volume, so density, defined as mass per unit volume, increases gradually down the group.

explain.title: The textbook's definition and trends
explain.body: “relatively soft metals with general trends down the group limited to decreasing melting point, increasing density and increasing reactivity.”

mistakes: Do not say that Group 1 reactivity decreases down the group; it increases.
Do not confuse the physical trends: melting point decreases, while density generally increases.
When explaining softness, include the reason: increasing atomic size weakens interatomic attraction.
Do not describe lithium, sodium and potassium as reacting with water at the same rate.
Remember that the Group 1 metals react with chlorine with increasing vigour down the group.

explain.title: Outer electrons and reactivity
explain.body: Group 17 elements have seven electrons in their outermost shells (ns², np⁵). They tend to accept one electron and form negative ions. Their reactivity decreases down the group because atomic size increases and the tendency to accept an electron decreases.

explain.title: Physical properties down the group
explain.body: Atomic radii, melting points and boiling points increase down the group. Larger molecules attract each other more strongly. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a fuming red-brown liquid, and iodine is a shiny grey solid that forms dark purple vapour when warmed.

explain.title: Oxidation, reduction and displacement
explain.body: Oxidation is a process in which an electron is lost. The substance which loses an electron is called a reducing agent. Reduction is a process in which an electron is gained and the substance which accepts the electron is called an oxidizing agent. Halogens are oxidising agents, and their oxidising power decreases in the order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. A stronger halogen can displace a weaker halogen from its compound.

explain.title: Hydrogen halides
explain.body: Halogens react with hydrogen to give hydrogen halides: H₂ + X₂ → 2HX. Bond length increases down the group, so the bond gets weaker and needs less heat energy to break. Therefore, thermal stability decreases in the order HF > HCl > HBr > HI.

mistakes: Do not reverse the trends: halogen reactivity and oxidising power decrease down Group 17.
Do not confuse oxidation with reduction: oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons.
Do not say that the weaker halogen displaces the stronger one. The stronger oxidising halogen does the displacement.
When explaining hydrogen-halide stability, include the full chain: larger halogen atom, longer and weaker bond, less energy to break it, lower thermal stability.
Use the exact order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ for oxidising power and HF > HCl > HBr > HI for thermal stability.

explain.title: Alkali metals
explain.body: Alkali metals have one outer electron and readily lose it to form positive ions. Their reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron becomes easier to remove. They are generally soft metals with low melting points.

explain.title: Halogens
explain.body: Halogens gain one electron to form negative ions. Their reactivity decreases down the group because the atoms become larger and attract an incoming electron less strongly. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from its salt.

explain.title: Metallic and non-metallic properties
explain.body: Strong metallic bonding makes metals generally strong, malleable and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals do not have this metallic bonding and may be gases or brittle solids.

explain.title: Transition elements and catalysts
explain.body: Transition elements show distinctive properties such as variable oxidation states, coloured compounds and catalytic activity. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

explain.title: Noble gases and physical states
explain.body: Noble gases are monoatomic and unreactive. Weak attractions between their atoms give them low boiling points. Halogen molecules become larger down the group, so their attractions increase and their physical states change from gases to liquid to solid.

mistakes: Do not reverse the trends: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group, while halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
Do not say that chlorine is less reactive than bromine; chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent.
In a redox question, distinguish the oxidising agent from the reducing agent: the oxidising agent gains electrons, while the reducing agent loses electrons.
Do not give a trend without its reason when the question asks “why”; link it to electron loss, electron gain, atomic size or bond strength.
When describing a catalyst, explain how it helps the reaction rather than saying it is used up.

notes.title: Group 1: the alkali metals
notes.answer: Group 1 elements are called alkali metals. Down the group, reactivity and density generally increase, while melting point decreases and the metals become softer.
notes.explanation: Group 1 metals become more reactive as you go down the group because their atoms get larger, so the outer electron is easier to lose. They also become softer, their melting points decrease, and their densities generally increase.
notes.simple: Going down Group 1, the atoms get bigger. Their outer electron is easier to remove, so the metals react more strongly.
examples: Lithium reacts steadily with water, while sodium reacts vigorously and potassium reacts violently.
The melting point falls from lithium (180 °C) to caesium (28 °C).
steps: Remember that Group 1 atoms have one electron in their outermost shell.
As you go down the group, atomic size increases.
The outer electron becomes easier to lose.
Therefore, reactivity increases down the group.
Also remember the physical trends: metals get softer, melting points decrease, and density generally increases.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does reactivity increase down Group 1?
notes.checkAnswer: Potassium reacts more vigorously than sodium because it loses its outer electron more easily.

notes.title: Group 17: Halogens
notes.answer: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent. It can displace bromine from a bromide solution.
notes.explanation: Group 17 elements are halogens. They have seven outer-shell electrons and tend to gain one electron. Their reactivity and oxidising power decrease down the group, while their atomic radii and the melting and boiling points increase.
notes.simple: Halogens usually gain one electron. The halogens near the top of the group gain it more easily, so they are more reactive.
examples: Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂.
Hydrogen bromide is less thermally stable than hydrogen chloride: HCl > HBr in thermal stability.
steps: Identify which halogen is higher in Group 17.
The higher halogen has greater oxidising power.
It can displace a lower halogen from a solution of its halide.
notes.checkQuestion: Which is the stronger oxidising agent, chlorine or bromine, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent, so it gains electrons and displaces bromine from bromide ions.

notes.title: Group Properties of Transition Elements
notes.answer: Transition elements are metals in groups 3 to 12. They often have high strength and high melting and boiling points, show variable oxidation states, and form coloured compounds. Some are used as catalysts.
notes.explanation: Transition elements are metals found in groups 3 to 12. They have properties such as high strength, high melting and boiling points, variable oxidation states, and coloured compounds. Some transition metals or their compounds act as catalysts in important industrial processes and in automobile exhaust systems.
notes.simple: Transition elements are metals in the centre of the periodic table. Some help chemical reactions happen faster as catalysts.
examples: Iron acts as a catalyst in the Haber process to produce ammonia.
Nickel is used as a catalyst to hydrogenate oils and make solid margarine.

notes.title: Properties of Noble Gases
notes.answer: Noble elements are group 18 elements; they are monoatomic gases with very low boiling points and very little chemical reactivity.
notes.explanation: Noble elements are the elements in group 18. They exist as single atoms, have very low boiling points and are mostly unreactive because their outer electron shells are complete. For example, helium has the configuration s², while neon has s²p⁶.
notes.simple: Noble gases are single atoms with full outer shells, so they hardly react.
examples: Helium is a noble element in group 18.
Neon has a complete outer shell with the configuration s²p⁶.
steps: Identify noble elements as group 18 elements.
Check that they exist as single atoms.
Recall that their outer shells are complete, except helium has s².
Link the complete outer shell to very little chemical reactivity.
notes.checkQuestion: Why do noble elements show very little chemical reactivity?
notes.checkAnswer: Noble elements are mostly unreactive because their outer shells are complete.

notes.title: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
notes.explanation: Metals and non-metals have different physical properties. Metals are usually strong, shiny, and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals are usually brittle and poor conductors. Graphite conducts electricity, and iodine is lustrous, so these are exceptions.
notes.simple: Metals are usually strong and conduct heat and electricity. Non-metals usually break easily and do not conduct them.
examples: Copper is a metal: it is lustrous and conducts electricity.
Sulphur is a non-metal: it is brittle and does not conduct electricity.
steps: Metals can be hammered into thin sheets; this property is called malleability.
Metals can be drawn into wires; this property is called ductility.
Non-metals are generally brittle, so they break when hammered or stretched.
Graphite is the exception among non-metals because it conducts electricity.
notes.checkQuestion: Which non-metal is an exception because it conducts electricity?
notes.checkAnswer: Metals are usually good conductors; non-metals are usually poor conductors. Graphite is an exception.

notes.title: Group Properties and Elements
notes.answer: Group 1 elements become more reactive down the group, while halogens become less reactive down the group.
notes.explanation: This chapter compares the properties and reactions of groups of elements. Down Group 1, metals lose their outer electron more easily and become more reactive. Down the halogens, atoms gain an electron less easily, so their reactivity decreases. Metals usually form positive ions, while halogens form negative ions.
notes.simple: Remember the opposite trends: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group, but halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
examples: Potassium reacts with chlorine to form potassium chloride: 2K + Cl₂ → 2KCl.
Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂.
steps: Identify the group of the elements in the question.
Recall the trend down that group.
Use the trend to compare the elements or predict the reaction.
For a reaction, write the balanced equation and identify any oxidising or reducing agent.
